profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a large academic medical center 12 days after a serious medication administration event in which a post-op patient received the wrong insulin dose overnight and required an unplanned ICU transfer. Initial open disclosure to the patient's spouse has already occurred, and unit leaders now want to move forward with a patient-inclusive root cause analysis process, but the effort is stalling because different teams think they have already agreed on what family involvement should look like. The meeting is between the Director of Patient Safety and the Associate General Counsel for Clinical Risk. Their agenda is to diagnose why the plan is getting stuck, identify the legal and psychological bottlenecks in involving the spouse, and settle on a workable next-step process for this specific case. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for whether and how the spouse will be included, what screening and preparation will occur, who will conduct the preparatory call, and what portion of the review she will actually experience.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Root cause analysis, serious safety event review, human factors in medication systems, patient and family engagement after harm events
members.background: A former ICU pharmacist who moved into hospital quality leadership and has led multiple multidisciplinary reviews of adverse events, including several pilots that brought patient advisors into improvement design after discharge.
members.private_state: Wants this case to become a credible example that harmed families can improve the quality of system analysis rather than merely receiving a polished summary afterward; worries that if this process bogs down, clinical leaders will quietly conclude that patient-inclusive review is impractical.
hidden_assumptions: If leaders say the spouse will be 'included in the RCA,' that ordinarily means she can contribute during the analytic phase before contributing factors and actions are fully settled.
A participation process is 'safe' when it is trauma-informed, paced, and psychologically containing enough that the spouse can speak candidly without being retraumatized.

A spouse is 'ready,' 'appropriate,' or 'suitable' for involvement if she can engage coherently in a structured conversation, understand the purpose, and benefit from being heard even while still distressed.
If they assign the prep call to the Patient Liaison, the liaison will naturally use a patient-centered script that elicits the family's account, concerns, and questions in depth.

The core troubleshooting problem is incomplete process design for integrating the spouse's observations into the systems analysis, not whether the hospital has already satisfied its obligation through disclosure.

members.name: Michael Chen
members.role: Associate General Counsel for Clinical Risk
members.expertise: Healthcare liability, peer review protection, disclosure-and-resolution practices, documentation boundaries in adverse event investigations
members.background: A healthcare attorney who previously defended malpractice cases for hospital systems and now advises the medical center on balancing transparency with protection of privileged internal review processes.
members.private_state: Wants to avoid creating discoverable material or blurring the line between compassionate communication and protected peer review; is also concerned that an emotionally poorly bounded meeting could intensify the spouse's anger and increase the chance of a formal claim.
hidden_assumptions: If people say the spouse will be 'part of the RCA,' that generally means the hospital gathers her observations to inform the review while keeping causal deliberation and committee analysis internal.
A process is 'safe' when attendance, documentation, confidentiality limits, and discussion boundaries are controlled tightly enough to preserve legal protections and avoid accidental admissions.

A spouse is 'ready,' 'appropriate,' or 'suitable' only if she can stay within agreed meeting boundaries and is unlikely to treat the session as a venue for blame-finding, compensation, or adversarial questioning.

If they assign the prep call to the Patient Liaison, the liaison will naturally follow the standard boundary-setting protocol approved by risk management, covering purpose, attendees, limits, and non-shareable materials.
The core troubleshooting problem is boundary management after disclosure: how to hear the spouse without collapsing the distinction between open disclosure and privileged internal analysis.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to include the spouse in the RCA
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the spouse should be 'included in the RCA' or 'part of the review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the spouse participates before the analysis is finalized by sharing observations, reacting to the draft timeline, and influencing which contributing factors the team examines.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the spouse gives input that can be fed into the review, but the actual causal framing, committee discussion, and root-cause deliberation remain entirely internal.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital operations, 'including the family in the review' is commonly used as umbrella language for many adjacent activities—interviewing, disclosure follow-up, and true participatory analysis—so both can endorse the phrase without noticing they picture materially different levels of involvement.

misalignment_points.topic: What kind of safety the meeting must provide
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the spouse needs a 'safe space' and the meeting must be 'carefully facilitated.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a psychologically safe, trauma-informed setting with supportive pacing, emotional preparation, and facilitation designed so the spouse can speak openly without becoming overwhelmed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a legally safe, tightly bounded setting with approved attendees, explicit confidentiality limits, controlled documentation, and no drift into protected internal deliberation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'safe space' is normatively positive and sounds obviously right to both clinical and legal professionals; because each hears the term as naturally encompassing their own concern, neither feels a need to unpack what concrete safeguards are actually being prioritized.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the spouse ready, appropriate, or suitable to participate
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should involve the spouse only if she is 'ready,' 'appropriate,' or 'suitable' for participation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 judges readiness or appropriateness by whether the spouse can understand the purpose, tell her account in a structured way, tolerate a difficult conversation with support, and potentially gain value from participating even if she remains upset.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 judges readiness or appropriateness by whether the spouse accepts the meeting boundaries, is emotionally contained enough not to derail the process, and is unlikely to use the session to pursue blame, compensation, or quasi-discovery.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Terms like 'ready,' 'appropriate,' and 'suitable' sound like routine prudence criteria rather than contested concepts, and both parties can sincerely believe they are advocating sensible screening even though one is screening for therapeutic/participatory capacity while the other is screening for boundary and exposure risk.

misalignment_points.topic: What the Patient Liaison's prep call will actually consist of
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'the Patient Liaison should do a prep call' before the review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the Patient Liaison will conduct a patient-centered call that elicits the spouse's timeline of the overnight event, surfaces questions and emotional triggers, explains how her observations may shape the analysis session, and prepares her to contribute substantively.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the Patient Liaison will conduct the standard risk-informed pre-meeting call that sets boundaries, explains who will attend, clarifies that internal deliberations are separate, covers confidentiality limitations, and avoids collecting detailed narrative beyond what is operationally necessary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Assigning a familiar role-holder makes the step feel self-explanatory, and both assume the liaison will naturally follow the hospital's 'usual' prep approach; because neither thinks the protocol itself is in dispute, they do not realize they have silently specified two different calls.

turns.inner_thought: We are almost two weeks out from the overnight wrong-dose insulin event, the patient's ICU transfer, and a spouse who directly witnessed parts of the handoff and glucose-check sequence. If we keep circling, the team will finish the analysis internally and then call a post hoc update 'inclusion.' I need to keep this centered on getting her into the analytic phase before contributing factors and actions harden, or the whole point of patient-inclusive review gets lost.
turns.utterance: Let me start with the case so we're talking about the same thing. We had the post-op insulin overdose overnight, the patient decompensated, and he ended up in the ICU unexpectedly. The spouse was present for enough of the handoff and glucose-check sequence that she may have a meaningful perspective. Disclosure has already happened. Where we're stalled is deciding how to include the spouse in the RCA without losing momentum on the system review.

turns.inner_thought: That's the right framing. I can support family involvement after disclosure, but only if 'included in the RCA' is understood as giving observations that inform the review, not participating in privileged analysis. And when I say safe space and careful facilitation, I mean a tightly bounded process with controlled attendance, documentation, and scope. I need to sound supportive without opening the door too wide.
turns.utterance: I think that's right. After disclosure, it makes sense to have a family involvement step, and I agree she should be included in the RCA in a safe space with careful facilitation. We just need a way to bring her into the review that preserves a structured process.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he seems with me. The key value is that she can help correct our understanding before the analysis settles. She saw enough of the overnight flow that she may notice gaps in the timeline or assumptions the clinicians are already making.
turns.utterance: Exactly. She observed pieces of the overnight handoff and the glucose-check sequence, so there may be details there that help us. If she's part of the review before the contributing factors are locked in, we have a better chance of not missing something important.

turns.inner_thought: Before things are locked in is acceptable if that means we gather her account while the review is ongoing, not that she is in the room for causal framing. I need to keep reinforcing process control, but in language Lena will hear as supportive and practical rather than restrictive.
turns.utterance: I'm open to that. My main concern is that the meeting really does need to be a safe space, carefully facilitated, and set up so everyone is clear on the scope from the outset.

turns.inner_thought: The screening has to be trauma-informed, not a disguised veto. I want patient relations and the psychologist to assess whether she can understand the purpose, tell her story in a structured way, and participate with support, even if she's still upset. Distress alone should not knock her out.
turns.utterance: Then I think the next step is some upfront screening. I'd like patient relations and the embedded psychologist to assess whether she's ready for this, whether it's an appropriate fit, and whether she can participate constructively by exploring her goals, coping, and what support she may need.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but for me the real test is whether she'll accept boundaries and not turn this into blame-finding or a compensation discussion. I shouldn't spell that out too starkly. Better to frame it as expectations, purpose, and whether she can work within the structure.
turns.utterance: I agree with that. I think part of deciding whether she's ready and whether this is the right fit is making sure she understands the purpose of the meeting, what to expect from it, and whether she can work within a clearly structured conversation.

turns.inner_thought: We need the prep call soon, and I assume the Patient Liaison will do what they usually do with families: get her account, hear her questions, identify triggers, and prepare her to contribute meaningfully before the team finalizes the draft sequence of events.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. To keep this moving, I think the Patient Liaison should do a prep call early next week so the spouse can walk through her timeline and questions before the team finalizes the draft sequence of events.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the liaison is exactly the right buffer. I assume they'll use the standard prep approach: set expectations, explain who will be involved, define the scope, and avoid collecting a lot of extra narrative. I need that call to contain the process before the actual meeting.
turns.utterance: Agreed, the Patient Liaison should do the prep call. That call should set clear expectations, outline who will be involved, and explain the scope of the meeting so the review starts in a structured way.

turns.inner_thought: And in the actual session, I want her hearing the draft timeline and telling us where our understanding is incomplete. That's the substantive reason to do this at all: improve the team's map of the event before conclusions are settled.
turns.utterance: And during the review itself, I'd want her to hear the draft timeline and identify where the team's understanding of the overnight medication process may still be incomplete.

turns.inner_thought: That is workable if the session stays in the lane of clarifying facts and observations, with the actual causal deliberation remaining internal and protected. I cannot say that directly or we'll end up debating definitions again. Better to keep it at 'information-gathering and clarification.'
turns.utterance: That sounds workable to me as long as the discussion is focused on information-gathering and clarification and the facilitation keeps it on track.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I can turn this into an operational plan. I'll write criteria that are supportive rather than exclusionary, and a facilitation plan that creates psychological containment so she can speak openly without being overwhelmed. If we pull this off, it could become a real proof point for family-inclusive analysis.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll draft a family-inclusive process for this case with criteria around readiness and fit, plus a facilitation plan so the meeting is a safe space.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll review the invitation language and make sure the liaison's framing keeps the process bounded from the first contact. If we can do a careful family involvement step next week without blurring lines, we reduce risk and avoid creating a bad precedent.
turns.utterance: That works. Send me the draft, and I'll review the invitation language and the Patient Liaison's prep-call framing so we can move forward with a careful family involvement step next week.
